abstract.p: Mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes the heavy chain of the actin-based molecular motor non-muscle myosin II-A (NM2-A), cause a spectrum of rare blood disorders collectively termed MYH9-related diseases (MYH9-RD). Previous data indicate that mutations in the motor domain result in more severe phenotypes than those in the dimerization/filamentation domain. Here, we show that N93K mutation, previously described as motor-impairing, has only a minor effect on myosin motor function in vitro, but it significantly enhances NM2-A filament stability and interaction with the chaperone UNC45a. When expressed in stress fiber-competent cells, e.g., COS7 or U2OS, and stress fiber-incompetent cells, e.g., MEG-01, NM2-A N93K formed amorphous aggregates that colocalized with wild-type NM2-A, NM2-B and UNC45a, but not F-actin, tropomyosin-4 or phosphoSer19, active, RLC. Another motor mutant, NM2-A R705H, caused milder defects in filament stability, adhesion maturation and aggregation in both types of cells. Conversely, the tail domain mutant NM2-A E1841K enhanced filament stability in COS7 cells without forming aggregates, while it promoted the formation of small, elongated aggregates in MEG-01 cells that did not co-localize with wild type NM2-A. These data indicate that the molecular defect caused by NM2A-N93K affects the distribution and function of the wild type allele, whereas NM2-A E1841K aggregates do not affect the wild type allele, which could constitute the molecular basis of the differences in severity in mutant MYH9 allele carriers.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Non-muscle myosin 2 (NM2) proteins are large filament-forming ATPases that generate intracellular force and motion on actin filaments, thereby enabling cellular processes such as cell migration, adhesion and division [1, 2]. At a molecular level, NM2 is a hexamer composed of two myosin heavy chains (MHCII) and four light chains. The MHCII is organized into four functional domains: a catalytic motor domain with binding sites for filamentous actin (F-actin) and adenine nucleotides at the N-terminus; a neck domain that binds the essential (ELC) and regulatory (RLC) light chains; a coiled-coil forming tail domain that allows two MHCIIs to dimerize and form filaments; and a short non-helical tail piece (NHT) at the very end of the C-terminus (Fig. 1A) [1, 2]. This protein complex (2 × MHCII + 2 × RLC + 2 × ELC) is frequently referred to as the NM2, or myosin, monomer. The motor domain binds to F-actin and uses the chemical energy derived from the hydrolysis of ATP to drive the movement of actin filaments. The neck domain binds the ELC and RLC and acts as a lever arm that translates small conformational changes in the motor domain into the power stroke, which drives actin filament movement [3]. RLC phosphorylation on Ser19 switches the NM2 monomer from a folded, filament assembly-incompetent (10S), autoinhibited conformation to an extended, assembly-competent (6S) conformation (Fig. 1A) [4–6]. 6S NM2 readily assembles into anti-parallel bipolar filaments (Fig. 1A). Bipolar filaments grow by lateral incorporation of additional NM2 subunits and fusion with established bipolar filaments to form larger filaments that contain up to 30 NM2 monomers in an anti-parallel configuration [7–9]. These filaments can concatenate both laterally and longitudinally to form long, contractile structures such as stress fibers in non-muscle cells [10].Fig. 1

Mammalian cells contain three MHCII genes that encode three heavy chain isoforms (MYH9, MHCII-A; MYH10, MHCII-B; MYH14, MHCII-C) with overlapping, but also specific cellular functions [11]. Their expression pattern is broad. Each cell type and tissue express higher levels of one isoform. For example, MHCII-B is the main isoform expressed in the central nervous system [12], while MHCII-A is the predominant isoform in hematopoietic cells [13]. The cellular functions of NM2 paralogs depend on their enzymatic activity, which is influenced by intrinsic and extrinsic regulatory events. Cellular contractility and actin dynamics also depend on the stability of the NM2 filaments, which is controlled by RLC phosphorylation-dependent conformational activation (discussed above) and also by phosphorylation of tail domain Ser/Thr residues and association with other proteins, e.g. S100A proteins [14, 15]. These control mechanisms define NM2 populations with specific cellular dynamics and functions despite a high degree of sequence conservation [2, 16–19].

Mutations in MYH9 cause a spectrum of blood disorders collectively termed MYH9-related diseases (MYH9-RD) [20, 21]. Patients carrying mutated alleles of MYH9 present different degrees of macrothrombocytopenia. Some also develop extra-hematological complications, including renal failure, deafness and presenile cataracts. The presence of NM2-A-containing aggregates (Döhle-like inclusions) in neutrophils serves as a sensitive diagnostic marker for MYH9-RD. Patients with mutations in the motor domain typically exhibit numerous small Döhle-like inclusions. Conversely, those carrying mutations in the coiled-coil or NHT domains tend to have larger inclusions [22, 23]. There is some correlation between the location of mutations in the MYH9 gene and both the severity of macrothrombocytopenia and the probability of developing extra-hematological complications. Mutations to the motor domain tend to cause the most severe phenotypes [24, 25].

In this study, we focused on missense mutation N93K, one of the first described mutations in NM2-A motor domain [26]. Early biochemical work on NM2-A N93K reported a defect in motor activity, an inability of the protein to move actin filaments and high susceptibility to aggregation based on cell-free experiments using a heavy meromyosin (HMM)-like fragment lacking the portions of tail domain involved in filament assembly [27]. These properties correlated well with the observed cytoplasmic inclusions reported in leukocytes of patients carrying this mutation [26]. NM2-A N93K still co-localized with F-actin in live cells [28], indicating that the mutation did not prevent NM2-A interaction with actin. The reported low ATPase activity and lack of motile activity of this mutant prompted several studies to use NM2-A N93K as a tool to differentiate between the enzymatic and non-enzymatic properties of NM2-A in various cellular processes, including focal adhesion turnover [29], filopodia formation [30], cytokinesis [31] and cell–cell interactions [32]. The rationale was that the cellular phenotypes rescued by NM2-A N93K would depend on a non-enzymatic activity, e.g. actin cross-linking, which does not require ATPase activity per se. Conversely, those that were not rescued would require an intact enzymatic (ATPase) activity. However, several reports cast doubts regarding the non-contractile nature of NM2-A N93K: (i) NM2-A N93K can restore almost every function lost in NM2-A-deficient or -null cells [28–34]; (ii) NM2-A N93K is sensitive to the small molecule inhibitor blebbistatin in cell biological experiments [31]; (iii) recombinant NM2-A N93K has an even higher unphysiological K+‧EDTA ATPase activity than wild type NM2-A [27, 31]; (iv) introduction of the equivalent amino acid substitution into the closely related NM2-B (N97K) results in soluble, enzymatically and functionally active protein in vitro [35]. Those reports led us to systematically revisit the alterations to the molecular function of NM2-A caused by the N93K mutation in parallel with other MYH9-causing mutations and engineered motors. Biochemical experiments with purified protein showed that the N93K mutation caused a minor defect in the motor function of NM2-A. In live cells, NM2-A N93K assembled into filaments similar to those of the native protein but featured a slower dynamic exchange of NM2-A N93K monomers in and out of filaments. They also localized more distally with respect to the leading edge compared to filaments made of wild type protein. The N93K mutation increased the interaction of NM2-A with UNC45a, a chaperone essential for NM2-A filament assembly and maintenance in cells [36]. Finally, we documented the distribution and cellular effects of expressing MYH9-RD-inducing NM2-A variants in stress fiber-competent cells, e.g. COS7 or U2OS, and stress fiber-incompetent cells, e.g. MEG-01. The distribution and filament dynamics of each NM2-A variant indicate that different MYH9-RD-inducing NM2-A variants display specific forms of aggregation in a cell type-dependent manner through diverse mechanisms that affect either the stability of the filaments and/or the dynamics of filament formation. This is also reflected in the shape and composition of the aggregates. Finally, our data strongly suggests the correlation between the differential effect of MYH9-RD-inducing NM2-A variants on the localization and/or function of the wild type allele and the heterogeneous degrees of severity and the onset of extra-hematological manifestations observed in mutant allele carriers.

sec.title: N93K is a bona fide molecular motor in vitro
sec.p: We revisited the impact of the N93K mutation on the kinetic and functional activity of NM2-A. First, we produced recombinant wild type NM2-A and NM2-A N93K in the baculovirus/Sf9 insect cell system for biochemical analyses. We then measured the steady-state ATPase activity of the proteins. We found that the steady-state ATPase activity increased as a function of the concentration of F-actin. The steady-state ATPase rate of NM2-A N93K at 100 µM F-actin (k100) is 0.07 ± 0.008 s−1, similar to the respective parameters of the wild type protein (0.09 ± 0.098 s−1) at the same actin concentration (Fig. 1B). Also, (-)-blebbistatin inhibits the steady-state ATPase activity of NM2-A N93K to a similar extent as the native protein with an IC50 of 2.7 ± 0.85 µM (NM2-A wild type) and 1.33 ± 0.25 µM (NM2-A N93K) (Fig. 1C). This result supports the in vivo observation that cytokinesis can be arrested after chemical inhibition of NM2-A N93K in a MHCII-B knockout background [31]. In addition, NM2-A N93K was able to propel actin filaments in an in vitro actin motility assay (Fig. 1D). Quantification of the gliding speeds results in velocities of 144 ± 29.7 nm·s−1 (wild type) and 103.5 ± 6.36 nm·s−1 (N93K). Finally, expression of MHCII-A N93K in COS7 cells, which do not express MHCII-A [37], showed that the RLC associated with NM2-A N93K was phosphorylated in Ser19 to levels comparable to those of the RLC bound to wild type NM2-A (Fig. 1E).

Since the molecular functions of NM2 are directly linked to its structure, we mapped the location of the N93K mutation within a structural model of the NM2-A motor domain based on the reported high-resolution structure of smooth muscle myosin 2 [38]. We found that the mutation site is surface-exposed and located in the N-terminal SH3 subdomain of the myosin motor domain where it likely interacts with W33, a residue implicated in MYH9-RD [39–41], and Q73 of the heavy chain (Fig. 1F). N93 did not engage in discernible interactions with structural elements of the active site or with regions comprising the actin-binding interface, including loop-2 and the helix-loop-helix motif (Fig. 1F), in agreement with the results from our biochemical analysis that show that NM2-A N93K is an actin-activated ATPase with similar activity to wild type NM2-A (Fig. 1B-D). Collectively, these results demonstrate that NM2-A N93K is a bona fide molecular motor when produced as a soluble protein in Sf9 insect cells. Thus, the reported cellular phenotypes in mammalian cells cannot be attributed to impaired catalytic activity.

sec.title: N93K is contractile in vivo but displays an altered subcellular localization in COS7 cells
sec.p:
To assess the contractile properties of N93K in live cells, we first compared its cellular behavior in parallel with an engineered, non-contractile NM2-A. We leveraged our previous finding that the tail domain of chimeric NM2 molecules governs their subcellular localization, filament dynamics, and role in focal adhesion turnover [37]. That study showed that a molecular chimera containing the head domain of MHCII-B and the tail domain of MHCII-A (MHCII-BH-AT) exhibited behavior comparable to that of wild type MHCII-A [37]. The introduction of the R709C mutation in the MHCII-B motor domain leads to an NM2-B form with reduced enzymatic and functional activity due to an increase in duty ratio [35]. This mutant binds to actin and exerts tension but does not support filament translocation [31]. Furthermore, the insertion of the R709C mutation into the native locus of the MYH10 gene impairs cytokinesis in vivo [42], suggesting that the lack of functionality in the motor activity translates into a functional deficiency in mutation-carrying cells. Thus, we reasoned that an engineered motor consisting of the head of MHCII-B with the R709C mutation, fused to the tail domain of MHCII-A (MHCII-BHR709C-AT) produces a bona fide non-contractile NM2 guided by the molecular cues that determine the cellular behavior of NM2-A (Fig. 2A). We then expressed GFP-MHCII-A wild type, MHCII-A N93K and MHCII-BH-AT in MHCII-A-negative COS7 cells and allowed them to spread on fibronectin. The expression of these three NM2-A variants increased actin bundling (Fig. 2B) as well as the number and size of focal adhesions (Fig. 2C-F), consistent with increased contractility. Wild type NM2-A and NM2-BH-AT produced similar effects, while NM2-A N93K displayed a slightly reduced ability to promote adhesion maturation (Fig. 2D) and assembly (Fig. 2E). Conversely, expression of GFP-MHCII- BHR709C-AT did not increase focal adhesion number or size (Fig. 2C-F), despite its prominent localization to stress fibers (Fig. 2B and C). Analysis of the subcellular localization of the fluorescent NM2 molecules with respect to lamellipodial actin (Fig. 2B) revealed that NM2-A N93K filaments were positioned farther from the leading edge than wild type NM2-A or NM2-BH-AT. In contrast, NM2-BHR709C-AT was located even farther from the leading edge, towards the center and rear of the cell (Fig. 2B-C, bottom rows and Fig. 2G). Together, these data indicate that NM2-A N93K exhibits contractile activity that promotes adhesion assembly and maturation in live cells, unlike the functionally impaired NM2-BHR709C-AT. However, NM2-A N93K has a reduced efficacy compared to wild type NM2-A or NM2-BH-AT in promoting adhesion assembly and maturation, indicating that the N93K mutation still causes a functional defect in vivo.Fig. 2

sec.title: MYH9-RD mutations stabilize NM2-A filaments in COS7 cells
sec.p:
To address the effect of the N93K mutation and other MYH9-RD-related mutations in the localization and dynamics of NM2-A, we first examined the localization of various EGFP-labelled NM2-A motors in COS7 (Fig. 3A), and U2OS (Fig. S1) cells spread on fibronectin. As described in the previous section, NM2-A N93K was positioned behind wild type NM2-A with respect to the leading edge. NM2-A E1841K, which causes May-Hegglin syndrome [43] and NM2-A R705H, which is also unable to move actin filaments in vitro [44], displayed a similar localization behind wild type NM2-A (Fig. 3A). Endogenous staining of NM2-B showed that NM2-A wild type localizes closer to the leading edge than NM2-B, as described [28]. Conversely, the NM2-A mutants appeared mostly intertwined with endogenous NM2-B (Fig. 3A). In U2OS (Fig. S1), the NM2-A variants still appeared closer to the leading edge than NM2-B, likely due to the formation of heterodimers containing endogenous NM2-A and the NM2-A variants. Such heterofilaments do not form in COS7 cells because they do not express endogenous NM2-A [37]. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) analysis of EGFP-labelled NM2-A N93K and NM2-A E1841K showed that both mutations enhance the stability of NM2-A filaments (Fig. 3B-D). NM2-A E1841K recovery was consistent with a previous report [45]. Conversely, the immobile fraction of NM2-A R705H was similar to that of wild type NM2-A (Fig. 3C and D), despite displaying a similar subcellular localization to that of NM2-A N93K or E1841K (Fig. 3A).Fig. 3

When we examined the effect of the NM2-A mutations on adhesion dynamics, we observed that, as seen before, NM2-A N93K had a decreased ability to promote adhesion formation (Fig. S2A). The ability of NM2-A R705H to promote adhesion formation was similar to wild type NM2-A, whereas NM2-A E1841K was a bit more efficient than NM2-A WT at promoting adhesion formation (Fig. S2A). Conversely, all three mutants examined displayed reduced adhesive area (Fig. S2B), which is a reliable readout for adhesion maturation (61). These data indicate that the effect of the mutants on adhesion maturation depends on the relative stability of the existing filaments and is largely independent of the effect of the mutations on the de novo nucleation of NM2-A filaments, which dominates its effect on adhesion assembly.

To further explore the effect of the N93K mutation on NM2 filament stability, we examined the ability of NM2-A to interact with the co-chaperone UNC45a, which assists in the folding of NM2-A as well as its assembly into filaments in vivo [36, 46–48]. Immunoprecipitation experiments revealed a greater association of UNC45a with NM2-A N93K compared to NM2-A (Fig. 4A and B). This finding was corroborated by reverse immunoprecipitation experiments (Fig. 4C and D). Additionally, intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ)-based mass spectrometric analysis (Fig. 4E) also indicated an increased interaction of NM2-A N93K with UNC45a. We also examined the interaction of UNC45a with NM2-A R705H and E1941K. We found that NM2-A R705H also displayed enhanced interaction with UNC45a, albeit to a lower extent than NM2-A N93K (Fig. S3A-B). To study if any of the mutations altered the half-life of the protein in live cells, we performed pulse-chase experiments using fluorescently labelled Halo-tagged MHCII-A, as previously described [49]. We observed that none of the mutations used in this study affected the decline of JF635 Halo ligand fluorescence over ten days (Fig. S4A-B), suggesting that the mutants are not more sensitive to degradation than wild type NM2-A over the duration of the experiment. Consistently, NM2-A N93K ubiquitination after 96 h was comparable to that of wild type NM2-A in cells left untreated or treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Fig. S4C).

Collectively, these data suggest that the N93K mutation does not alter the kinetic activity or susceptibility to degradation of mutant NM2-A. Instead, it induces subtle structural changes that translate into a strengthened interaction with UNC45a. Together with published FRAP data showing that exchange of NM2-A N93K in filaments is significantly slower than wild type [28], these data indicate that the mutation increases its residence time in filaments, potentially by remaining bound to filament-associated UNC45a for longer periods of time.

To understand the mechanism that underlies the altered 10S-filament transition in N93K, we generated a model of the interacting heads motif of NM2-A in the 10S conformation based on our recent, high resolution cryo-EM structure of smooth muscle myosin-2 [38]. In this structure, both motor domains, referred to as the blocked and the free head, are docked against each other and interact with the myosin tail that is folded in three places to adopt the compact autoinhibited conformation. We found that, in the wild type protein, N93 in the blocked head interacts with Q73 in the blocked head and R1417 located in segment 2 of the folded myosin tail. In N93K, the interaction between K93 with Q73 and R1417 would be repulsive, which likely results in the destabilization of the 10S structure (Fig. 5). Together with the steric clash of K93 with W33 described in Fig. 1F, structural modeling supports the possibility that the N93K mutation destabilizes the 10S conformation, which could in turn favor the stabilization of the NM2-A variant in filaments.Fig. 5

sec.title: MYH9 mutants cause mutation-specific aggregation phenotypes
sec.p:
While performing the FRAP and adhesion experiments described in Fig. 3 and Fig. S2 in COS7 cells, we noticed that the NM2-A variants occasionally formed amorphous, non-filamentous aggregates in these cells (Fig. 6). There were two types of aggregates: high expressors displayed non-linear accumulation of fluorescence in central structures of the cell, although colocalization with HSP90B, a classical ER marker [50], is only partial (Fig. S5). Conversely, some cells displayed cytoplasmic aggregates (Fig. 6A) that were larger in NM2-A N93K and smaller in NM2-A R705H expressing cells (Fig. 6A, arrowheads). Aggregates were not observed in cells expressing NM2-A wild type or E1841K (Fig. 6A), despite being expressed at comparable levels (Fig. S6). Quantification of cytoplasmic aggregates revealed that this was a rare occurrence in COS7 cells (Fig. 6B). To gain insight into the formation of the aggregates, we characterized their molecular composition. We found that, in addition to NM2-A (Fig. 6C, column 1 and Fig. S5), they also contain UNC45a (Fig. 6C, column 2) but not F-actin (Fig. 6C, column 3) or HSP90B (Fig. S5). Importantly, UNC45a was only present in aggregates made of NM2-A N93K and R705H to a lesser extent (Fig. 6D, columns 1–2,4). Cytoplasmic NM2-A aggregates also contained endogenous NM2-B (Fig. 6D, column 2,4), but not TPM4, which was mainly in present in lamellipodia (Fig. 6D, column 3,4). In addition, we observed that NM2-A aggregates did not contain Ser19-phosphorylated RLC (Fig. 6E, column 2,4). This suggested that aggregates formed when NM2-A was dissociated from F-actin. These cells can be differentiated to produce platelet-like particles [54], thus they constitute a useful model to study protein aggregation in this context. However, likely due to their leukemic nature, these cells do not form stack-like, NM2-A-containing structures similar to those reported in primary mouse megakaryocytes [55]. Instead, they display a diffuse localization of NM2-A similar to that of T lymphocytes [56]. We examined the localization of Halo-labelled mutant NM2-A and mNeonGreen-tagged wild type NM2-A using stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy in cells categorized as either low or high expressors (Fig. 7A). To investigate whether NM2-A N93K formed small, sub-resolution aggregates, we applied Spatial Image Correlation Spectroscopy (ICS) to a subset of STED images collected from high expressors (Fig. 7A). Due to the requirements of the analysis (see Material and Methods), we focused on small regions devoid of large aggregates as those shown in Fig. 7C. ICS analysis confirmed that the size of the particles (represented as intensity, Fig. 9A-D) and degree of aggregation (Fig. 9E-H) of NM2-A E1841K in these regions were higher than those of wild type NM2-A (Fig. 9D), indicating that this mutant aggregated even at low concentrations. In agreement with this observation, the number of measurable particles per area unit, represented as density (Fig. 9I-L), was lower in the case of NM2-A E1841K (Fig. 9L). Similar observations were made for N93K and R705H, but the differences in intensity and degree of aggregation, while still significant, were less pronounced than in the case of E1841K (Fig. 9B-C, F-G), suggesting that the critical concentration required for aggregation is higher for these variants. NM2-A N93K and NM2-A R705H densities were also lower than WT, but again less than NM2-A E1841K (Fig. 9J-K). As a control, we performed measurements in cells expressing two forms of wild type NM2-A, labelled with mNeonGreen or labelled with Halo-tag. Halo-tagged NM2-A WT intensity appeared slightly higher than that of mNeonGreen-labelled NM2-A wild type, which can be attributed to the different spectral properties of JF635 Halo ligand and mNeonGreen (Fig. 9A). Conversely, degree of aggregation was very low (Fig. 9E), whereas density was similar (Fig. 9I). This indicates that the tag (Halo or mNeonGreen) influences the cellular behavior of the molecule, but to a very modest extent. Notably, the degree of aggregation of mNeonGreen-labelled NM2-A wild type in Halo-tagged NM2-A N93K-expressing cells was not significantly different from cells expressing Halo-tagged wild type NM2-A, although it trended towards increased aggregation (Fig. 9N). Conversely, the degree of aggregation of mNeonGreen-labelled wild type NM2-A in cells co-expressing Halo-tagged NM2-A E1841K was significantly lower than in cells co-expressing Halo-tagged wild type NM2-A or NM2-A N93K (Fig. 9N), indicating that this variant does not form aggregates with wild type NM2-A, as also indicated in Fig. 7C.

In summary, the N93K mutation drives NM2-A to form abnormal aggregates in a concentration-dependent manner in MEG-01 cells. UNC45a and wild type NM2-A also localize to those aggregates. In contrast, the E1841K mutation endows mutant NM2-A with an intrinsic, concentration-independent ability to form a different type of aggregates that do not sequester wild type NM2-A. STED ICS revealed that these properties were indeed concentration dependent and manifested at a molecular level even when aggregation is not detectable using conventional superresolution microscopy.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Here, we show that NM2-A carrying the N93K mutation is a bona fide molecular motor with in vitro ATPase and actin motility activity. This observation is in line with various cellular studies that did not report major differences between NM2-A N93K and wild type in processes such as focal adhesion maturation, phagocytosis, and cytokinesis [28, 29, 31, 34, 57]. The results herein do not challenge the separation of the molecular functions of the head (motor) and tail (dimerization/assembly) domains of NM2 [58–60]. Instead, they support the notion that mutations in the motor domain may affect filament assembly. This could be accomplished by alterations to the head–tail interactions that maintain NM2 in a folded, filament assembly-incompetent 10S conformation outside of filaments. While the in vitro kinetic and functional signatures of N93K are similar to those of the native protein, we found that N93K causes defects in the localization and the turnover of NM2 filaments in adherent COS7 cells, while large concentrations of protein carrying the mutation cause protein aggregation in megakaryocytic cells. Since the catalytic activity of NM2-A N93K is similar to that of wild type NM2-A, the only explanation for the observed increased filament stability is that N93K may alter the conformational dynamics of the NM2-A monomer during filament assembly/disassembly. In this model, the increased residence time of NM2-A N93K in large filamentous structures such as stress fibers would be due to a potentially decreased ability of mutant NM2-A to adopt the 10S conformation (Fig. 1A). This is supported by structural modeling of the 10S state, which suggests that its stability is reduced by the onset of the N93K mutation due to steric clash with W33 and altered electrostatic interactions with Q73 and R1417 of segment 2 of the folded tail compared to wild type.

In this regard, synonymous mutations to N93K (N97K) and R1417 (R1421) in the closely related smooth muscle myosin 2 have been reported and described in Uniprot (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P35749).

Here, we found that NM2-A N93K aggregation is concentration-dependent in both stress fiber-competent and -incompetent cells. In stress fiber-competent cells, NM2-A E1841K forms normal-looking filaments that only display slight abnormalities in terms of subcellular localization and dynamic behavior. Conversely, expression of the same NM2-A variant in stress fiber-incompetent cells drives the formation of worm-like aggregates even at low concentrations. This agrees with a previous study showing that NM2-A E1841K formed abnormally long, over-assembled filaments in vitro [55]. NM2-A E1841K aggregates do not recruit wild type NM2-A or UNC45a, suggesting that this mutant does not form heterofilaments with wild type NM2-A, and/or that filaments containing the mutant NM2-A tend not to co-assemble with wild type filaments. Our data suggests that in platelets, which only contain NM2-A, NM2-A N93K would sequester wild type NM2-A into aggregates, impairing not only its own function, but also contraction produced by the wild type allele. Conversely, in carriers of the E1841K mutant, NM2-A E1841K and NM2-A wild type would form separate filaments, hence the native protein could still execute its cellular functions correctly, but the total contractile capacity of the cell would be reduced. These data justify that patients carrying the N93K mutation exhibit a more severe phenotype than E1841K carriers, in agreement with the established model that mutations in the motor domain of NM2-A cause the most severe phenotypes [24].

The formation of large aggregates observed in NM2-A N93K-expressing cells indicates that N93K is amongst the most detrimental MYH9 mutations, which may explain its scarcity among MYH9-RD patients [61]. Interestingly, another rare mutation in the motor domain, R705H, exhibits a reduced degree of aggregation and has less dramatic effects on filament stabilization despite localizing in the same spatial region as N93K.

We also found that NM2-A N93K and R705H interact more strongly with UNC45a than NM2-A wild type or NM2-A 1841 K. UNC45a plays two fundamental roles in the biology of NM2-A: i) it is necessary for proper hexamer biosynthesis in the ER [62]; ii) it provides support for NM2-A assembly in stress fibers [36]. While these functions are likely related at a structural level, their functional significance is different. The ER-localized interaction between NM2-A and UNC45a is involved in the renewal of the pool of cytoplasmic NM2-A, whereas the stress fiber-localized interaction enables NM2-A assembly and turnover. It is likely that increased interaction of NM2-A N93K with UNC45a results from the increased residence time of NM2-A N93K in filaments. However, this cannot be the only reason since NM2-A E1841K also has an increased residence time in filaments, yet its interaction with UNC45a is normal. Our data indicates that NM2-A N93K-containing aggregates (and R705H to a lesser extent) also contain UNC45a, which could be a major source of increased interactions. Our data does not rule out the possibility that the mutations increase, or modulate, the affinity for UNC45a directly during the last steps of NM2-A hexamer biosynthesis in the ER or elsewhere in the cytoplasm. The map of UNC45a-muscle myosin 2 interaction recently reported [48] indicates that most interactions between UNC45a and myosin 2 occur in the head domain, supporting this hypothesis.

Due to the generation of steric clashes and potential alterations of electrostatic interactions within the motor domain (Figs. 1F and 5), we propose that the N93K mutation interferes with the ability of the NM2-A monomer to return to the 10S conformation. This would be particularly important during monomer dissociation from filaments. A possibility is that, during filament turnover, dissociating monomers do not return to a properly folded conformation and instead tend to form non-filamentous aggregates. This would be consistent with the lack of phospho Ser19-RLC and F-actin in the aggregates. In this context, it is tempting to speculate that the aggregates described here are similar to Döhle-like inclusions seen in neutrophils from MYH9-RD patients [22]. However, our data clearly establishes that mutations to different segments of the MYH9 gene trigger diverse aggregation phenotypes. The increased susceptibility of NM2-A N93K to form aggregates may also account for the discrepancies between the findings presented in this study and previous reports [27]. Members from most myosin classes have been recombinantly overproduced and purified from baculovirus-infected Sf9 insect cells [63]. Mammalian NM2s were among the first myosins that were purified in large quantities in this expression system [16–18, 27, 35, 64]. Occasionally, NM2 paralogs were reported to be insoluble when overproduced in Sf9 cells from a virus that was generated from a pVL1392 vector backbone [64]. The expression of soluble protein could be restored by re-engineering the expression construct at the DNA level in a pFastBac1 vector backbone after removing an out-of-frame upstream start codon, indicating that the vector backbone as well as cloning strategy affects protein production [35]. The initial report on the production of NM2-A N93K heavy meromyosin suggests that 0.2–2% of the total produced protein could be extracted, though the protein was produced at levels comparable to WT from a PVL1392 vector backbone [27]. The reported protein yield is with 10 mg/4 × 109 cells ~ 5–10 times higher than the average protein yield from bacmid-transfected cells [27]. Though the precise reason for the insolubility of NM2-A N93K in previous in vitro experiments remains elusive, we speculate that the strong overexpression in Sf9 cells may have exhausted the cellular folding capacity. Consequences of these nonoptimal expression conditions may have caused protein damage, misfolding, and aggregation of NM2-A N93K in previous in vitro studies [27].

In summary, the results described here are consistent with the N93K mutation perturbing the conformational equilibrium of NM2-A, rather than affecting its kinetic activity. This supports the notion that the N93K mutation triggers NM2-A aggregation by perturbing the conformational plasticity of NM2-A. This mechanism of aggregation is different from that triggered by mutations in the rod domain of MHCII-A, which seem to alter mutant NM2-A filament dynamics by stabilizing rod-to-rod interactions.

sec.title: Plasmids
sec.p: cDNA constructs of full-length MHCIIA (amino acids 1–1960, Uniprot: P35579) or subfragment-1 (amino acids 1–836, Uniprot: P35579) were cloned into a modified pFastBac1 vector carrying the coding sequence of FLAG-tag via restriction-free cloning. The N93K mutation was introduced via site-directed mutagenesis. The cDNA of the RLC (Uniprot: A0A8V0ZIV3) and ELC (Uniprot: P60661) were inserted into a pFastBac vector via restriction-free cloning. CMV-based GFP-MHCII-A wild type and GFP-MHCII-A N93K have been described previously [28]. GFP-tagged MHCII-A R705H and E1841K were obtained by site-directed mutagenesis. FLAG-, mNeonGreen- and Halo-tagged versions as indicated throughout the text were obtained by overlapping PCR. Briefly, forward primers were specific of the N-terminus of the tag (FLAG, mNeonGreen or Halo), and reverse primer contained the single BsiWI target sequence in MYH9 (nucleotides 575–580 of the CDS of human MYH9 gene, Gene ID: 4627). The GFP-MHCII-B/A chimera has been described [37]. GFP-MHCIIBR709C/A was obtained by site-directed mutagenesis on the MHCII-B/A-containing plasmid. UNC45a-GFP was a generous gift from Pekka Lappalainen (U. Helsinki) and has been described elsewhere [36].

sec.p: The following antibodies were used: MHCII-A (RRID:AB_2734686, Biolegend); MHCII-B (RRID:AB_2749903, Biolegend); UNC45a (RRID:AB_2039010, Enzo Biosciences); FLAG (RRID:AB_2616449, Merck); GFP (RRID:AB_627695, Santa Cruz Biotechnology); paxillin (RRID:AB_1603632, abcam); Ubiquitin (RRID:AB_3065231, CST); GRP94/HSP90B1 (RRID:AB_2233347, Proteintech); TPM4 (RRID:AB_425723, Abnova); phosphoSer19-RLC (RRID:AB_330248, CST). sec.title: Other reagents
sec.p: Fibronectin (F2006) from human plasma, (-)-blebbistatin (B0560), MG-132 (ref. 474790) and anti-FLAG-M2-conjugated beads (RRID:AB_2637089) were from Merck. sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: Sf9 cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 12659017) were maintained in Sf-900 III SFM medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 27ºC in suspension culture. COS7 cells (RRID:CVCL_0224, ATCC CRL-1651), HEK-293 (RRID:CVCL_0045, ATCC CRL-1573) and U2OS (RRID:CVCL_0042, ATCC HTB-96) cells were maintained in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin and 1% non-essential amino acids. MEG-01 (RRID:CVCL_0425, ATCC CRL-2021) cells were maintained in RPMI1640 medium supplemented with 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin, 1% NEAA and 10% FBS. Cells were routinely sub-cultured when 80% confluent (2 × 106/ml for MEG-01) and used for a maximum of 20 passages.

sec.title: Native and recombinant protein production
sec.p: FLAG-tagged human NM2A or N93K full-length or subfragment-1 protein were produced together with the ELC and RLC in the baculovirus/Sf9 expression system as recommended by the manufacturer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The recombinant protein was purified via FLA-affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography on a HiLoad 16/600 Superdex 200 pg as described [16, 66]. Actin was prepared from rabbit skeletal muscle acetone powder (Pel-Freez Biologicals) as described [67].

sec.title: Steady-state ATPase assay
sec.p: The steady-state ATPase assay was performed as described earlier [68], using 0.5 µM of the constitutively active subfragment-S1 NM2-A WT or NM2-A N93K at a temperature of 25 °C in buffer containing 10 mM MOPS (pH 7.0), 50 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 2 mM ATP, 40 units/ml lactate dehydrogenase, 200 units/ml pyruvate kinase, 1 mM phosphoenolpyruvate, and 0.2 mM NADH in the presence of 0–100 µM actin in a Cary 60 spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies). The effect on (-)-blebbistatin (SelleckChem) on the actin-activated steady-state ATPase activity of NM2-A WT or NM2-A N93K was assayed at a fixed actin concentration of 100 µM. Errors are reported as mean ± SEM.

sec.title: In vitro motility assay
sec.p: The in vitro motility assay was performed as described previously at a temperature of 30 °C with RLC-phosphorylated full-length NM2-A or NM2-A N93K in buffer containing 50 mM KCl, 20 mM MOPS, 0.1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP, 50 mM DTT, 2.5 mg/ml glucose, 0.05 mg/ml glucose oxidase, 2 µg/ml catalase [69]. Actin filaments were labeled with rhodamine phalloidin. The movement of actin filaments was analyzed with CellTrak (Motion Analysis). Filaments that showed a velocity standard deviation/velocity ratio larger than 0.33 were excluded from the analysis.

sec.title: Homology modeling
sec.p: The structure of the human NM2-A motor domain was modeled using the structure of the motor domain of human NM2-C (PDB ID: 2YCU) in the pre-power stroke state as a template in Modeler [70]. The structure of human NM2-A in the autoinhibited state was modeled using the cryo-EM structure of smooth muscle myosin II (PDB ID: 7MF3) as a template in Modeler.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence, imaging and focal adhesion quantification
sec.p: COS7 cells were transfected with the indicated plasmids and incubated for 48–72 h. 105 cells were allowed to adhere to a #1.5H, 12 mm round coverslip coated with 2 µg/mL human fibronectin for 3 h. Cells were subsequently fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Pierce Thermo) in PBS for 10 min, rinsed three times in TBS and stained with an anti-vinculin antibody (1:5000 in buffer IF) followed by goat anti-mouse AlexaFluor568 (Invitrogen, 1:2000 in IF buffer) and phalloidin-AlexaFluor647 to illuminate focal adhesions. Cells were observed in a Leica Thunder Tissue Analyzer equipped with a 63 × objective (NA 1.45) and appropriate LED laser lines and filters for EGFP and AlexaFluor568 imaging. Images in Fig. 3A and S1 were collected in a Leica confocal SP8 microscope equipped with a white laser and a HC PL APO 100 ×/1.40 OIL objective. Images (30 per condition in three independent experiments) were collected using LAS X and focal adhesions quantified as described [66, 71]. Distance of the NM2-A variant-containing filaments to the leading edge was measured using ImageJ from the outer edge of lamellipodial actin to the closest detectable orthogonal pixels of fluorescence corresponding to NM2.

sec.title: Mass spectrometry and data analysis
sec.p: Samples were lysed with 2 × SDS protein sample buffer (40% glycerol, 240 mM Tris/HCL pH 6.8, 8% SDS, 0.04% bromophenol blue, 5% beta-mercaptoethanol). Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and stained using InstantBlue® Coomassie Protein Stain from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Protein spots between apparent Mw 60–300 kDa were excised from the gel and digested with trypsin according to published procedures [63]. A “control” piece of gel was cut from a blank region of the gel and processed in parallel with the sample. The peptides resulting from tryptic digestion were acidified with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to obtain a final concentration of 0.2% and purified by reverse phase chromatography in Empore C1879 microcolumns [64]. The liquid phase was removed, and the gel pieces were completely dried in a vacuum centrifuge SpeedVac from Eppendorf. Gel pieces were resuspended for its analysis by mass spectrometry in 0.5% formic acid (FA) 2% acetonitrile (ACN). Samples were acquired by reverse phase liquid chromatography (LC), using a nano UPLC system from NanoAcquity, Waters, connected to a TIMSTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker). Peptidic elution was done using a gradient from 2 to 35% of ACN and 0,1% FA in 30 min in a Trap AcclaimPepMap 100 C18 precolumn from ThermoFisher and a C18 1.9 μm 75 ID 15 cm column from Bruker fifteen. Acquisition was performed in a positive mode using a data dependent method (DDA), using PASEF. To get a 100% working cycle, 100 ms were set for the ramp and the accumulation time of the electric field gradient. The acquisition method used topN acquisition cycles, with a full frame acquisition m/z -ion mobility and 10 PASEF MS/MS, each PASEF with an averaging of 12 MS/MS spectra, resulting in a total time of 1.1 s. MS spectra were acquired between 2 and 5 loadings, MS and MS/MS spectra were acquired from 100 to 1700 m/z, precursors for PASEF were selected by the PASEF algorithm. A polygon filter was applied to the area m/z—ion mobility to exclude precursors with a single charge and low m/z from PASEF selection. Precursors were examined in an ionic mobility range (1/K0) of 0.6–1.6 Versus/cm2, for which a minimum precursor signal was established to be considered 2,500 and a "target value" of 20,000 to reprogram MS precursors for PASEF MS/MS. The analysis of the data obtained was carried out with MaxQuant v. 1.6.17.0 [65], using the Andromeda algorithm against the entire Homo sapiens proteome database (UP000005640) from Uniprot (March 2021) and common contaminant sequences included in the program Maxquant. The search parameters were tryptic digestion up to 2 failed cuts: “first search” and “main search” of 20 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively. Methionine oxidation and protein N-terminal acetylation were established as variable modifications and cysteine carbamidomethylation as fixed modification. For the identification of peptides and groups of proteins, peptides with a minimum of six amino acids in length with 1% FDR 80 at the peptide and protein level obtained by means of the search strategy against a library of reverse sequences were considered. To calculate the relative abundance of each protein, the iBAQ algorithm [66] was used, which is obtained by adding the intensity of all the observed peptides of a protein divided by the number of theoretically observable tryptic peptides of that protein, providing a ranking of the relative abundance of the different proteins within a sample.

sec.title: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP)

sec.p: HEK-293 cells (2 × p100/condition) were co-transfected with equimolar concentrations of plasmids encoding FLAG-MHCII-A variants and UNC45a-GFP [36]. After 48 h, cells were resuspended in 1 mL lysis/MgATP buffer. Lysates were incubated at 4ºC for 15 min, clarified by centrifugation at 14000 × g. Then, clarified lysates were incubated with 10 µL of either GFP-trap, or FLAG-M2-magnetic beads for 120 min at 4ºC under continuous stirring. Magnetic beads were rinsed three times with 1 mL lysis/MgATP buffer and resuspended in 100 µL 1 × Laemmlii buffer. The levels of the associated molecule (MHCII-A or UNC45a) were assessed by Western blot and densitometric quantification using ImageJ.

sec.title: Expression of MHCII-A proteins in MEG-01 cells
sec.p: MEG-01 cells were collected, centrifuged at 300 × g and resuspended at 2 × 107 cells/mL in cold OptiMEM medium. 200 µL of cellular suspension were mixed with 10 µg of the indicated plasmids in a 1:1 proportion (5 µg of mNeonGreen-MHCII-A WT and 5 µg of Halo-MHCII-A mutant) and electroporated in 0.2 cm-gap cuvettes (Thermo) in a nucleofector I device (Lonza) using program X-005. Immediately after the pulse, cells were resuspended in RPMI1640 medium containing 20% FBS and incubated at 37ºC. After 48 h, cells were incubated with JF635 (1:3000) for 45 min to label Halo+ cells; centrifuged at 160 × g and sorted in a FACSAriaIII (BD Biosciences). Cells were divided into “low Halotag” and “high Halotag” gates as shown in Fig. 7A. Negative cells were discarded. After 4 h recovery, cells were allowed to adhere to #1.5H round coverslips coated with 25 µg/mL fibronectin in the presence of 100 ng/mL PMA (Santa Cruz Biotechnology). Cells were allowed to adhere for 45 min and fixed in 4% PFA (in PBS). For endogenous UNC45a staining, cells were permeabilized with Triton X-100 0.1% in TBS for 10 min and incubated overnight with a 1:1000 dilution of anti-UNC45a antibody (Proteintech), followed by a 1:2000 dilution of goat-anti-rabbit-AlexaFluor568. Dilutions were carried out in PHEM buffer (10 mM PIPES, 300 mM Sucrose, 100 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1 mM EGTA) supplemented with 1% BSA and 100 µg/mL human immunoglobulins. Coverslips were mounted using Prolong Glass (Invitrogen). Images were obtained in a Leica TCS SP8 STED 3X microscope, fitted with an HC PL APO 100 ×/1.40 OIL STED WHITE objective. Acquisition was always performed in sequential mode to prevent cross-depletion: step 1) 15% white laser power with 75% power from the 775 nm STED laser (JF635 depletion); step 2) 10% white laser power at 561 nm with 60% depletion from the 660 nm STED laser (only performed for UNC45a co-staining, that is, AlexaFluor568 depletion); step 3) 10% white laser power at 491 nm with 70% depletion from the 592 nm STED source (mNeonGreen depletion). 1024 × 1024 images with a 25 nm/pixel size were captured and processed in LAS X and ImageJ for display (as in Fig. 7) or further processed by ICS (see below). For co-localization analysis (Fig. 8B), we hand-picked 4–5 64 × 64-pixel regions per cell and Pearson correlation coefficient was estimated using the Coloc2 script in Fiji.
